title: Havdalah
hookLine: a braided candle, sweet spices and wine separate holy time from the week

lines: A BOX OF SPICES, PASSED AROUND.
cards: Saturday night. Someone goes to the window, looks up, and counts: one star, two, three. Shabbat is over.
But nobody grabs their phone yet. The lights stay low. Someone lights a tall candle with several wicks braided together, and it burns with a big, bright flame, like a small torch.
A child holds it up high. There's a cup of wine, filled so full it spills over. And a little box of cloves or cinnamon goes from hand to hand, and everybody breathes in.

teach.b: Havdalah means separation, distinction. Shabbat began with Kiddush over a cup, making the time holy. It ends with Havdalah over a cup, marking where holy time stops and the ordinary week starts.

Four blessings: over the wine, over the spices, over the fire, and one praising God for separating, which names a list of separations, among them holy and ordinary, light and darkness, the seventh day and the six days of work.
Why spices? There's a teaching in the Talmud that on Shabbat a person receives an extra soul, a neshamah yeteirah, a bigger capacity for rest and joy.
When Shabbat leaves, the extra soul leaves too, and later teachers say the spices are there to revive you, a little sweetness for the loss. Why fire?
Fire can't be kindled on Shabbat, so the first thing you do when it ends is make light.
A story in the midrash says Adam, on the first Saturday night of the world, afraid of the dark, was given the wisdom to strike two stones together and make the first fire.
The candle has several wicks because the blessing speaks of the lights of fire, plural.
People hold their hands up to the flame and look at the light on their fingernails, using the fire for something before blessing it. Then the candle goes out in the spilled wine, with a hiss.

Often a song follows for Elijah the prophet, who tradition says will one day bring the final redemption, and everyone wishes each other shavua tov, a good week. The week begins, but you walk into it smelling of cloves.

how: On Saturday night after three stars appear, Jews say Havdalah over a cup of wine, fragrant spices and a braided candle, then extinguish the candle in the wine and wish each other shavua tov.

o: a cheerful welcome home for a traveler
marking off holy time from the week as Shabbat ends
a prayer of mourning said at the end of a week

games.q: what's inside the separation — tap the pairs.
p: revive you as the extra soul leaves
use the light before blessing it

s: Kiddush begins it; Havdalah ends it, separating holy time from the week.
the Talmud speaks of an extra soul on Shabbat
the neshamah yeteirah; the spices comfort you as it leaves.
the Havdalah candle has one wick
it's braided from several, because the blessing speaks of the lights of fire.

games.q: Shabbat is over. you've just lit the braided candle and said its blessing. what do people do with their hands?
o: hold them up and look at the light on their fingernails.
games.why: they hold their hands to the flame and look at the light on their fingernails, using the fire before blessing its light.

practice: Pick up something fragrant near you, a spice jar, a lemon, coffee, a flower, soap, or if there's nothing, remember a scent you love.
Bring it close and breathe it in slowly, thinking of what you'd like to carry from your rest into your busy days: some patience, some quiet, some sweetness. Breathe in once more, as if storing it.

wordCard.voice: Havdalah. Separation: wine, spices and a braided flame on Saturday night, marking where holy time ends and the week begins.

orig.note: Hebrew: separation, distinction. the blessing praises the one who separates holy from ordinary.

carryVoice: Your line: carry the scent in. Tomorrow a new part begins: blessings through the day. Day one hundred eight, done.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 54a; Genesis Rabbah 11:2 (Adam's first fire)
